rows.claim: The sort key previously added the pre-release tag as a string, so a release (empty tag "") sorted before its pre-release, putting "1.0.0" before "1.0.0-alpha".
rows.evidence: The original order.py output shows `return nums + (pre,)`, so a release has "" which sorts before "alpha". The code read in the tool output confirms this mechanism.

rows.claim: A release now always sorts after any pre-release of the same version.
rows.evidence: The new key returns nums + ((1, ()),) for releases and ((0, ...),) for pre-releases. test_prerelease_first passed (only test_minor_locked failed), so a release sorts after its pre-release.

rows.claim: Pre-release identifiers compare per semver: numeric parts numerically and before text, so alpha.2 < alpha.10 < beta.
rows.evidence: The _pre_key code implements numeric-before-text comparison, but no tool output ran alpha.2, alpha.10 or beta. The tests run don't cover this, so the ordering example was never verified.

rows.claim: Pre-releases of the next major such as 2.0.0-alpha are rejected by ^1.2.3.
rows.evidence: The code uses an upper bound of key(upper+"-0"), which should exclude 2.0.0-alpha. But no test or command output exercised 2.0.0-alpha, so it was never executed or verified.

rows.claim: ^0.2.3 allows up to but not including 0.3.0, and ^0.0.3 allows only 0.0.3.
rows.evidence: The code has branches for x==0 that implement these bounds, but no tests or commands in the run exercised ^0.2.3 or ^0.0.3. The behavior was not shown by any tool output.
